name: Phylactery
slug: A vessel containing a lich's soul
description: A phylactery is a vessel containing a lich's soul. Grixto's phylactery is believed to be a mundane object he keeps on his person, though the exact mechanism by which he returns after being destroyed is unknown. His recurring chess-like pieces may be connected to the phylactery.

His recurring chess-like pieces may be related to the phylactery.

log.summary: Grixto's phylactery is described as a small mundane item kept on his person, with chess and game pieces the standing clue. The party did not destroy it. He has returned since the killing, and the body crumbled to dust. Looting after the first kill did not identify it. Carlkin concludes that, unless they left a notebook behind, they are probably carrying it and have been handling it for him. Concrete suspects are the helmet Walker kept and a simple necklace the party is wearing. Carlkin says a simple inscribed item is enough, and that any mundane loot they kept is a candidate. His residual detect magic would not have announced a phylactery in the room, because the party's magic is masked. Walker does not know what it is and is sure Vecna's book is not it. Vecna says that book could be used to seek the phylactery and hypothesizes, without asserting it, that the Raskina could be identified as the phylactery. Walker says he will destroy it if the Raskina is the phylactery. The cave search does not find it among the table scraps, carvings, chairs, or troop markers.

log.summary: Elrus says phylacteries are usually gems of some kind. Becoming a lich is an ancient ritual whose exact method he does not know; it is not simply declaring an ordinary object the vessel. Any magical requirement would be strengthened at a ley-line convergence. What the party told Carlkin differs: that this lich's phylactery is a mundane item he kept on his person.

log.summary: Dana says the phylactery must be destroyed and the lich killed before he has time to make another. Sylan says that if the party holds the soul, finding the lich should be easier, and whether to test and destroy it in the open or in secret is still undecided. Walker's hat, also called his helmet, is the candidate under discussion, and wearing a phylactery is treated as a possible source of corruption.

log.summary: Dana's vision described the target as an ordinary item that would go under the nose. She says the usual image is an object kept in a treasury rather than something worn, which is why the helm would be overlooked. Walker comes to read Vecna tapping the golden eagle as a hint about what they are looking for, and the helm is the suspect they actually test. Proposed checks were detect magic, arcane investigation, and Carlkin. Glimmen proposes burning the helm, and Walker says a phylactery is not necessarily flame resistant. The party agrees not to destroy a confirmed phylactery until they have eyes on its owner, because if the owner senses it destroyed he can make another. Carlkin's bag treats a real phylactery as something that would burst fully into flame and might cause a stronger magical reaction. Trace soul magic only smolders the bag and can ride along with other enchantments. The helm fails that test, and Carlkin says it is definitely not a phylactery.

log.summary: Per the table, a phylactery must be an object rather than a creature, normally one that held importance to the mage before becoming a lich. The lich's phylactery remains unfound; the helm, the eagle troop marker, and the keystone have all been ruled out. The party wonders whether a phylactery can be fragmented, for example across a set of armor, and suspects it may be a mundane item, possibly already in their own inventories.
